content.title: About
content.content: A muffin is a small, individual-sized quick bread, usually sweet, made from a batter of flour, eggs, sugar, milk and leavening agents. The batter is often enriched with butter, berries, nuts or chocolate and baked in a cup-shaped mold, giving it a characteristic domed top.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first muffin recipes appeared in England in the 19th century as "English muffins," but the modern sweet version originated in the United States in the early 20th century.
Muffins are popular as a convenient breakfast or snack because they are easy to take on the go.
There are over 100 flavor variations: blueberry, chocolate, banana, nutty, lemon‑glazed, and more.
Muffin batter is typically thicker than cake batter, helping the muffins keep their shape during baking.
In some regions muffins are served with cream cheese frosting or fruit coulis.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates in muffins provide quick energy, making them a handy snack before physical activity.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Flour and eggs supply B1, B2, and niacin, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Protein content
items.content: Eggs and dairy add both animal and plant protein, supporting tissue repair.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Milk and butter contribute calcium and vitamin D, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Antioxidants in berry versions
items.content: Blueberries, raspberries or strawberries add anthocyanins that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweet muffins can raise blood glucose levels and contribute to weight gain if eaten frequently.

items.title: Saturated fat load
items.content: Butter and some oils increase calorie density and may affect cholesterol levels.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Common ingredients include eggs, milk and wheat, which can trigger allergies in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional muffins contain wheat flour, making them unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Muffins can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, split and spread with cream cheese, nut butter or jam. They are often paired with tea or coffee. For a healthier option, use whole‑grain flour, reduce sugar, and add fresh fruit.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer keeping, refrigerate up to 5 days or freeze in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 3 months. Warm them in the oven or microwave before serving.
